Qur'an 4:156 states: “They say: ‘We put the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, God's Messenger, to death,’ whereas they did not kill him and did not crucify him; it only appeared so to them […] Rather, God raised him to Himself.” Because this verse approaches the teaching of the Acts of John (cited above, n. 127), we must emphasize that this teaching is much subtler than the usual, straightforward conception of Docetism—or, at least, the oversimplified account commonly given of it—as the belief that Christ had only a semblance of a body and suffered only in appearance. In truth, the “Docetism” of the Acts of John is, above all, a theological critique of knowledge itself. Recall C. G. Jung's words: “Historical facts are real, certainly, but they reveal only what impresses the man of the senses and what he can conceive. For the person who knows the divine mysteries, however, the event of the crucifixion is more than this: it is a Mysterium—a symbol expressing a parallel psychic event that takes place within the contemplative person. In Platonic terms, it is an event in a heavenly place: on a mountain and in a cave where a Cross of Light stands [Acts of John 97 ff.], a cross with many synonyms—that is, many aspects and meanings. It expresses the unknowable nature of the ‘Lord’ […]. Understood in this way, the Docetism of the Acts of John appears rather as a fulfilment of the historical fact, far from diminishing its value” (Von den Wurzeln des Bewusstseins, Zurich, 1954, p. 331). We would add that Docetism simply gives voice to the experience reported in the Acts of Peter: “I saw him as I was able to grasp him” (Eum vidi qualem capere potui). Each divine appearance, or theophany, is measured by the “dimension of the soul”: by its capacity to allow a divine Figure to appear to it. Ultimately, the soul does not witness an event outside itself; it is the place where the event happens. Likewise, in our phenomenology, knowledge is not knowledge about Being: it is Being knowing itself. ↩

See Ernst Benz's article cited above, p. 157, n. 128, and the new edition of his major work Ecclesia spiritualis, Stuttgart, 1964. It would be highly worthwhile to bring out certain shared features of Joachim of Fiore's interpretation through corresponding biblical figures and events, and the spiritual interpretation practiced in Shiite theosophy. Just as there is a correspondence between events and figures in the Old and New Testaments, so too there is a correspondence between different periods in the complete cycle of prophecy, with the same protagonists appearing on a continuing plane of sacred history. There is also a correspondence between the cycle of the prophetic mission (nobowwat) and the cycle of the Imams' walâyat. As the Old and New Testaments stand to the “Spiritual Gospel,” so the Torah and Gospel stand to the Qur'an. Since the Imam was secretly commissioned alongside every prophet, Shiite esotericism understands itself as gathering together all earlier inward teachings and bringing them to the flowering of their truth. Some Shiite writers themselves have identified the Paraclete—the reign of the Spirit—with the Twelfth Imam. There is an affinity between the “archetype of the Book” (Omm al-Kitâb) and the Evangelium aeternum, or Eternal Gospel. On both sides, spiritual interpretation takes a prophetic form. We have occasionally used the phrase Ecclesia spiritualis (“spiritual church”) above for the hidden hierarchies of the Shiite community. There is nevertheless a difference. Given the Twelfth Imam's present concealment (ghaybat), the Shiite community cannot cross that boundary; whereas devout enthusiasts tried to bring Joachim of Fiore's Ecclesia spiritualis “into history,” and tragedies ensued. ↩

See our article “Pour le huitième centenaire d'Alamût” (cited above, p. 77, n. 52). Concerning the “Great Resurrection” proclaimed at Alamût on 8 August 1164, we recalled there the formula Resurrectio non est factum historicum sed mysterium liturgicum: “The Resurrection is not a historical fact but a liturgical mystery.” It can be understood by anyone for whom “liturgical mystery” has more reality than any historical fact. See Piotr Hendrix's penetrating analysis, “Der ‘Garten’ und der ‘Morgen’ als Ort und Zeit für das Mysterium Paschale in der Orthodoxen Kirche,” Eranos-Jahrbuch XXXII, Zurich, 1964, p. 151. ↩

Recall J. A. Bengel's rule of interpretation: Te totum applica ad textum, rem totam ad te (“Apply your whole self to the text, and the whole matter to yourself”), a golden rule in harmony with the young Luther's spirit. Compare this rule from Suhrawardî's Kalimât al-tasawwuf: “Recite the Qur'an as though it had been revealed for your case alone.” The two interpreters, one of the Bible and one of the Qur'an, speak here in striking unison. ↩

All this also shows that the supposed theological “demythologization” leads only to a dead end of ignorance. Compare Friedemann Horn's suggestive article “Swedenborgs Vision einer Neuen Christenheit,” Offene Tore 2 (1957), p. 43, recalling how Thomas Mann, in Joseph und seine Brüder, seeks to make historical events transparent. He shows how biblical figures “led back” earthly events—the etymological meaning of ta'wîl—to their supraterrestrial form, their heavenly truth, which does not abolish earthly reality but instead grounds and guarantees it. We may take Swedenborg's statement as a golden rule: “All angels receive the Heaven outside them according to the quality of the Heaven within them” (De Caelo et Inferno, § 55). ↩

For the Shiite interpretation of John 15:26, a Gospel verse known to our authors, see Haydar Âmolî, Jâmi' al-asrâr (above, n. 29), pp. 103–104, and Ibn Abî Jomhûr, Kitâb al-Mojlî, p. 308. See in the same place the ta'wîl that 'Abdorrazzaq Kâshânî, a follower of Ibn 'Arabî, gives of the letters ALM preceding the Qur'an's second sura: the three letters refer respectively to the divine Self (dhât), the archangel Gabriel as Holy Spirit and Active Intelligence, and the Twelfth Imam, Mohammad ibn Hasan 'Askarî, as the origin, centre, and completion of being. ↩

Recall that Ibn Bâbûyeh, known as Shaykh Sadûq, was one of the pillars of Shiite theology in the fourth/tenth century (d. 381/991). His writings were vast, but only a relatively small number of treatises survive. Each is an immensely precious collection of traditions (hadîth and akhbâr) from the Imams. Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, an eminent philosopher and theosopher of the Safavid period (d. 1103/1691–1692), devoted a profound, closely argued commentary to Sadûq's Kitâb al-Tawhîd. Unfortunately, the work remained unfinished, though its three volumes total more than a thousand pages. ↩
Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, commentary on the Tawhîd, Chapter II, second hadîth, fol. 27 (Persian manuscript). ↩

See our study “Le Temps cyclique dans le mazdéisme et dans l'ismaélisme” (Eranos-Jahrbuch XX), Zurich, 1952, pp. 182 ff., comparing ideas of time and temporality in Proclus, Rhazes, Nâsir-e Khosraw, and Bîrûnî. ↩

Ibid., Chapter II, third hadîth, fol. 43: “Know that everything in the world of Molk [the visible kingdom] has its own Malakût [spiritual kingdom]; and this Malakût in turn has a Jabarût [higher realm of divine power] that rules over and encompasses it […]. In short, every being has a divine Word, a divine Command that watches over it and guards it.” The names given to the three universes corresponding to the three kinds of time vary. We may find the world of appearances ('âlam al-shahâda), the world of mystery ('âlam al-ghayb), and the world of the Mystery of Mystery ('âlam ghayb al-ghayb); or the world of created things ('âlam al-khalq), the world of the divine Command ('âlam al-Amr), and the world of divinity ('âlam al-olûhîya); or the world of visible dominion ('âlam al-molk), the world of divine lordship ('âlam al-robûbîya), and the world of divinity ('âlam al-olûhîya). Ibid. ↩

This explains why a traditional Eastern historian understands his work as that of a chronicler: faithfully recording and placing side by side the chains of testimony (isnâd). It is wrong to reproach him for failing to offer a critical overview of historical phenomena and their “causes.” He—or someone else—may develop a philosophy of history elsewhere, but not in the chronicle. In our own tradition, by contrast, historians sometimes construct a philosophy of the facts in the very act of reporting those “facts.” ↩
On this inseparable relationship between prophetic religion and mystical experience, see our entire L'Imagination créatrice dans le soufisme d'Ibn 'Arabî, Paris, 1958. ↩

See especially Kolaynî's Kitâb al-Hojjat (in Osûl min al-Kâfî), Chapter II, together with Mollâ Sadrâ's extensive commentary, Sharh al-Osûl min al-Kâfî, folio edition, Tehran, n.d., pp. 447–448. See our paper “Imâmologie et philosophie” at the 1968 Strasbourg conference on Imami Shiism (above, p. 65, n. 46); also below, pp. 240 and 306, nn. 221 and 295. ↩

Saffâr Qommî, Basâ'ir al-Darajât, Tabriz, 1381, Part I, Chapter XII, pp. 28–29. Saffâr Qommî (Abû Ja'far, or Abû'l-Hasan Mohammad ibn Hasan ibn Farûkh) was among the best-known Imami transmitters of tradition. A disciple of the Eleventh Imam, Hasan 'Askarî (d. 260/874), he was one of Ibn Bâbûyeh's sources. He died in Qom in 290/903. See Rayhânat al-adab, vol. II, p. 483, no. 873. ↩

Qur'an 28:88 states: “Everything is perishable except His Face.” What it means to say that this Face is the Imam, and in what sense the Imam is the imperishable Face within every being, is shown by a long discussion by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, equally important for philosophy and spirituality. See our study Face de Dieu et Face de l'homme (above, p. 54, n. 25). In Chapter VII below, we shall mention a corresponding interpretation given by a shaykh of our own time. ↩

On the Fourteen Ideal Realities as temples of tawhîd (the divine oneness), see also Pénétrations, pp. 217–218, n. 101; for the order of their emergence on the different levels of being, see Terre céleste, pp. 111 ff. ↩
See Kolaynî, Kitâb al-Hojjat, cited edition, pp. 10 and 20–21; Pénétrations, § 124, p. 204 of the French translation, and n. 96, pp. 213–214. ↩
On the hidden spiritual hierarchies, see the references given above, pp. 121 ff., nn. 91–93. ↩

Ibid., p. 200, n. 88. The Ismaili philosopher Abû Ya'qûb Sejestânî also addresses the question in his Kashf al-Mahjûb (The Unveiling of Hidden Things), edited by H. Corbin (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 9), Tehran–Paris, 1949, using a precise Persian vocabulary: hast-kardan, “to bring into being”; hast-kunendeh, “that which brings into being”; hast-kardeh, “that which has been brought into being.” Kunendagî, the condition of that which brings into being, transcends being itself: being is always the being of what has been brought into being, the hast of the hast-kardeh. ↩

This is the hadîth referred to above in n. 151. Sayyed Kâzem Reshtî's commentary on the Throne Verse (Sharh Âyat al-Korsî, Qur'an 2:256) is a dense work that unfortunately remained unfinished: lithographic edition, Tabriz, n.d. (around 1860), quarto, 352 pages. These few lines from its prologue are worth quoting: “Know that the Qur'an is a writing in cipher, a symbolic story [ramz] between the Friend and the Beloved; no one but those two knows the true meaning of what it says.” ↩

For simplicity, both korsî and 'arsh have been translated here as “throne,” although the terms refer to two distinct metaphysical realities. Their relationship resembles that between the empyrean heaven (corresponding to 'arsh) and the firmamentum, the heaven of the fixed stars (corresponding to korsî). Note, too, a difference in the use of “Light of Lights” (Nûr al-anwâr). Among the Ishrâqîyûn (philosophers of illumination), the term means the First Being, which is also the supreme Being (Ens supremum) and the source of emanation. Here, the “Light of Lights” is the First Being understood as the first created being (protoktistos), because the creative Principle transcends being, including the first being it brings into existence. Imami and Ismaili gnosis agree on this metaphysics of being, which calls for a rigorous “first philosophy.” See above, p. 200, n. 159, and Pénétrations, pp. 235–236. ↩

Sayyed Kâzem Reshtî, op. cit., p. 2, and Pénétrations, pp. 218–220. The image of the Throne and its four lights goes back to the Imams' own teaching. See Kolaynî, Kitâb al-Tawhîd, Chapter XX (the chapter on 'Arsh and Korsî); Safînat, II, p. 616; and Pénétrations, pp. 213–215. The Throne motif—corresponding in Islamic gnosis to the Merkabah (divine chariot or throne) in Jewish Kabbalah—has a constant fourfold structure, though the symbolic lights and the names of the four higher archangels (Seraphiel, Michael, Gabriel, Azrael) are assigned in somewhat different ways. See our book on Ibn 'Arabî, pp. 270–271. All our theosophical authors discuss this motif; coordinating the details would require a whole book. Above this archangelic group of four stand the four Malâ'ika al-a'lûn, or Angeli Sublimes (“Sublime Angels”). Two are the Spirit of the divine Command; the other two have charge of the angels of the Veils (the Cherubim, Karûbîyûn). See Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, Ziyârat, p. 117. ↩
See above, p. 55, n. 27, and p. 196, n. 155; Pénétrations, p. 121. ↩
See Pénétrations, pp. 166–167 (translations of two texts by Mîrzâ Ahmad Ardakânî Shîrâzî and Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î). ↩

The hadîth from which the phrase quoted in the main text is taken appears in Rajab Borsî's Kitâb Mashâriq al-Anwâr (The Orientations of the Lights), from the eighth/fourteenth century. It is regarded as one of the most difficult hadîth: a visionary conversation between the Imam's divine dimension (lâhût) and human dimension (nâsût). We have so far found and studied six commentaries on it; see Annuaire 1968–1969, pp. 150–151. For the Throne's fourfold structure, found at every level of being, see Mollâ Sadrâ's commentary, Sharh, p. 314. The Imam declares: “Nothing God has created in His Malakût lies outside these four. We recalled earlier that every species contains four inner things [omûr bâtinîya]: a nature, a sensory soul, an imaginative soul, and an intellect. These have many dwellings and many forms in which they appear …” ↩

Explaining a hadîth of the First Imam—“I am in relation to Mohammad as light is in relation to light,” that is, lumen de lumine (“light from light”)—Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î writes: “This light is wholly in Mohammad; wholly in Imam 'Alî; wholly in Fâtima; wholly in Imam Hasan; wholly in Imam Hosayn; and likewise in each of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. For although it has become multiple, it is one. That is what the Imams mean when they say: ‘We are all Mohammad. The first of us is Mohammad. The one among us in the middle is Mohammad. The last of us is Mohammad.’” See Pénétrations, p. 102. ↩

The corresponding Ismaili assertion, derived from negative theology, is that the only divine Selfhood accessible to human beings is the First Intelligence's knowledge of its own Principle—even if that knowledge is expressed negatively. See Trilogie ismaélienne, pp. 19–20, nn. 24 and 26. Here, what we know of God is the knowledge God has of His Creation and of Himself within the Haqîqat mohammadîya (the eternal Muhammadan Reality). The knowledge possessed by this Reality is not knowledge about God, but God's own knowledge of this Reality or Logos. ↩

This is the text cited above, p. 201, n. 160; see Sharh Âyat al-Korsî, p. 2. The text cited above, p. 205, n. 166 also shows how the Fourteen Immaculate Ones are fourteen persons of light (ashkhâs nûrânîya), yet each is at once the very person of Mohammad, the “Friend of God.” Each is therefore also the whole Haqîqat mohammadîya, both individually and together with all the others. It is remarkable that a kind of kathenotheistic conception—each divine figure appearing in turn as supreme—is already found in a proto-Ismaili text such as Omm al-Kitâb, edited by W. Ivanow in Der Islam, vol. 23, Leipzig, 1936. An Italian translation was recently published by Pio Filippani-Ronconi, Naples: Istituto universitario orientale, 1966. The master ('Abdallâh Sabbâh) ceases to see the young Imam (Moh. Bâqir) and instead sees the Prophet transfigured, his face encircled by a halo of luminous hair: “I am the Lord, pure and beyond every attribute and description.” He then sees 'Alî and, after him, Fâtima. Dressed in silk and gold brocade, with a green veil over her hair, she declares: “There is no God but me, no God in divinity or humanity, in the heavens or on earth, except me, Fâtima the Creator [in the masculine: Fâtima-Fâtir]. It is I who created the spirits of the True Believers.” Finally, Imam Hasan appears, then Imam Hosayn, who declares: “I am Hosayn ibn 'Alî, I am Hasan ibn 'Alî, I am Fâtima the Radiant [Fâtima al-Zahrâ]; I am 'Alî al-A'lâ [the Most Exalted]; I am Mohammad the Chosen” (manuscript fols. 19b–22; see Italian translation, pp. 18–20). ↩
See Kâzem Reshtî, Sharh Âyat al-Korsî, p. 3, and above, p. 81, n. 55, and pp. 102 ff., nn. 73 and 75. ↩
Ibid., pp. 3–4. This title or form of address appears at the opening of the original Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a and itself comes from earlier hadîth. ↩
On the connection between hikâyat, understood as “mystical narrative,” and sacred history (hierohistory), see above, n. 132. ↩

Ibid., pp. 3–1 [range as transcribed in the French; probably defective]. We have referred above (p. 102, n. 73, and p. 203, n. 162) to the higher angelic hierarchies: al-Malâ'ika al-moqarrabûn, al-Karûbîyûn, and al-A'lûn. They were not required to bow before Adam, since they were the very lights shining within him. Iblîs (Satan) was not one of them, hence the question put to him after his refusal: “Are you swollen with pride, or could you be one of the Sublime Ones?” (Qur'an 38:76). ↩

Unfortunately, we must limit ourselves here to very few references. A comprehensive, systematic study of the Qur'an's spiritual interpretation has yet to be written. It would need to bring together the principles formulated and applied by thinkers such as Haydar Âmolî and Semnânî. Mollâ Sadrâ commented on the “Throne Verse” not only in his commentary on Kolaynî's Kâfî, but also in a separate work published in his Tafsîr. Although that commentary covers only a few suras, it fills no fewer than 617 folio pages (Shiraz, 1286/1869). Such a study should begin with the rules of interpretation laid down by the Imams themselves. Rûzbehân Baqlî recalls them at the opening of his mystical Tafsîr ('Arâ'is al-Bayân fî haqâ'iq al-Qorân, Bombay, 1301). We referred above (p. 201, n. 160) to Sayyed Kâzem Reshtî's work, whose opening pages concern spiritual interpretation generally. Another important work by Reshtî is his “Epistle on the Levels of the Outward, the Inward, and Symbolic Interpretation” (Risâla fî maqâmât al-zâhir wa'l-bâtin wa'l-ta'wîl), in Majmû'a, a collection of thirty-four treatises, lithographic edition, Tabriz, 1276/1859–1860, pp. 366–368. ↩

For further details, see our earlier studies: Avicenne et le Récit visionnaire (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 4); Étude préliminaire pour le Livre des deux Sagesses de Nâsir-e Khosraw (ibid., vol. 3); Trilogie Ismaélienne (ibid., vol. 10); and the study cited above, n. 4, our first comparative outline of the principles of interpretation used by Swedenborg in Arcana caelestia and Qâzî No'mân in Asâs al-ta'wîl. ↩

We should also mention the very interesting and original approach of Sayyed Ja'far Kashfî (d. 1267/1850–1851), a Shiite theosopher of the previous century. He distinguished three levels—tafsîr, ta'wîl, and tafhîm—which he aligned respectively with three philosophical schools: the Peripatetics, the Stoics, and the Ishrâqîyûn, or Platonists. We shall return to this below; see vol. III, Book IV, Chapter I, n. 49. ↩

See the epistle mentioned above, p. 212, n. 175, at the end. Its author briefly explains zâhir (the outward or exoteric meaning), zâhir al-zâhir (the outward meaning of the outward), bâtin (the inward or esoteric meaning), and bâtin al-bâtin (the inward meaning of the inward). Ta'wîl applies the hadîth of Imam Ja'far (above, p. 188, n. 151) to perceive meanings at the level of the microcosm, the mesocosm (alchemy), and the macrocosm. More generally it applies the Prophet's famous hadîth on the seven inward depths of the Qur'anic text (see vol. III, Book IV, Chapter II below): hence seven zâhir, seven zâhir al-zâhir, seven bâtin, and seven bâtin al-bâtin (7 × 4 = 28, corresponding to the twofold nature of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones). Semnânî had calculated the overwhelming number of volumes that would be needed to comment on the entire Qur'an in the way he had begun, starting with Sura 53 (“The Star”), where he continued the work of Najm Dâyeh Râzî (see vol. III, Book IV, Chapter IV below). ↩

See our Histoire de la philosophie islamique, I, pp. 53 ff. On pp. 19–20 of that work, the rules of spiritual interpretation stated by the First and Sixth Imams are the very rules Rûzbehân invokes at the start of his Tafsîr (above, n. 175). ↩

We have already repeatedly referred to Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr and Tafsîr al-Borhân (the usual short title; more fully, Kitâb al-Borhân fî tafsîr al-Qorân) (above, p. 27, n. 4). We must also name Tafsîr-e Sharîf-e Lâhîjî, by Qotboddîn Ashkevârî (a pupil of Mîr Dâmâd, d. 1630), published in four large volumes by Moh. Ibrâhîm Âyetî and Jalâloddîn Mohaddeth, Tehran, 1381. There are others besides. Yet none of these commentaries brings together all the traditions of the Imams concerning every verse. ↩

A solitary researcher who undertakes that task can only work himself to death. We noted above (p. 27, n. 4) Hosayn Yazdî's great Tafsîr, which gathers the Imams' traditions verse by verse, yet whose eight folio volumes reach only the end of Sura 2. The manuscript is preserved in the library of Shaykh Abû'l-Qâsim Ebrâhîmî (Sarkâr Aghâ) in Kerman. Also unpublished are the extensive commentaries of Semnânî and of Sayyed Ahmad 'Alawî, Mîr Dâmâd's pupil and son-in-law (Latâ'if-e ghaybî). Later we shall recall how, thanks to Mr Osman Yahya, the author's own manuscript of all seven large volumes of Sayyed Haydar Âmolî's Shiite Sufi Tafsîr—also unpublished—was recently rediscovered (see vol. III, Book IV, Chapter I below). ↩

The ideal complete work would be a Tafsîr that gave, for every verse of every sura, its zâhir, bâtin, and other levels of meaning. Semnânî clearly understood this challenge and provided an example. Especially valuable in this respect is a collection of commentaries on several suras by shaykhs of the Shaykhi school, published in Kerman, 1379–1381 (500 + 307 pages). The following suras are treated, each in terms of its zâhir, ta'wîl, and bâtin: al-Tawhîd (112) by Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î; al-Hojorât (49) by Moh. Karîm Khân Kermânî; al-'Ankabût (29), Fajr (89), and Kawthar (108) by Moh. Khân Kermânî; and al-Jomo'ah (62) and al-Monâfiqûn (63) by Zaynol-'Âbidîn Khân Kermânî. ↩

We should nevertheless draw attention to Qâzî No'mân's great work Asâs al-ta'wîl (The Foundation of Spiritual Interpretation). Each chapter systematically gathers the Qur'anic verses relating to a particular prophet; part of it is studied in our Herméneutique spirituelle comparée (above, n. 4). See also Ismailitischer Korân-Kommentar (Mizâj al-tasnîm), edited by R. Strothmann, fascicles 1–4, Göttingen, 1944–1955, covering Sura al-Tawba (9) through Sura al-'Ankabût (29). ↩

This alludes to the stages of the alchemical operation (solve et coagula, “dissolve and coagulate”) symbolizing the transformation of the spiritual person. We should recall here the “hadîth of the tomb.” The tomb represents philosophy itself: the place where the outward aspect of revealed religion and its doctrines must undergo decomposition and death, to rise again in the garden of gnostic truth. See our Histoire de la philosophie islamique, I, pp. 115–116. See also Commentaire de la Qasîda Ismaélienne d'Abû'l-Haytham Jorjânî (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 6), Tehran–Paris, 1955: Arabic text of the “hadîth of the tomb,” with Persian commentary, p. 79, and French translation in the introduction, p. 48. ↩
See the epistle cited above, n. 175, at the end, and n. 178. ↩

We have often referred to Kolaynî's great work, al-Kâfî (above, p. 29, n. 15, and p. 57, n. 31), which systematically organizes the teachings of the Imams. Mohammad ibn Ya'qûb ibn Ishaq Kolaynî Râzî came from a prominent family in Ray (ancient Rhages, roughly twelve kilometres south of Tehran), where he became the shaykh and pîshvâ (spiritual guide) of the Shiites. Leaving behind that distinguished position and the relative advantages Shiism enjoyed in Ray, he moved to Baghdad (around 309/921), seat of the Abbasid caliphate and an inhospitable city for Shiites. He had the courage to do so because of his great undertaking: to move closer to the sources and assemble the extensive corpus of traditions that would sustain his fellow believers for centuries. He lived long enough to know at least the last nâ'ib, or representative, of the Twelfth Imam: 'Alî al-Samarrî, whose death in 329/940, only months apart from Kolaynî's own death in Baghdad, also marked the beginning of the “Great Occultation” (al-ghaybat al-kobrâ; see Book VII below). ↩

One can appreciate the scale of this literature by leafing through the newest bibliographical inventory of Shiite writings: Shaykh Aghâ Bozorg Tehrânî, Dharî'at ilâ tasânîf al-shî'a, published in Tehran and Najaf. Eighteen volumes had appeared by 1968, listing titles only as far as the end of the Arabic letter lâm. ↩

Conditions were particularly difficult for the Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh Imams. The last two, Imam 'Alî Naqî and Imam Hasan 'Askarî, were kept under more or less continuous detention by the Abbasid authorities in the military camp of Samarra, about a hundred kilometres north of Baghdad. But we must remember that if the Fifth and Sixth Imams, Mohammad Bâqir and Ja'far Sâdiq, seem more prominent than the others because of the extent and importance of their teaching, it is not because they were “greater.” All twelve Imams share the same essence and are equal. Rather, the decline and fall of the Umayyads and the rise of the Abbasids (751) briefly made conditions less difficult for the Fifth and Sixth Imams. That is why Imam Ja'far could have so many pupils. One may judge the wider situation from the records of conversations preserved by Ibn Bâbûyeh in his 'Oyûn akhbâr al-Imâm al-Rezâ. ↩

“Not a single verse of the Qur'an,” says the Imam, “came down to God's Messenger without his making me recite it and dictating it to me. I then wrote it in my own hand, and he taught me its tafsîr [literal explanation] and its ta'wîl [spiritual interpretation], what abrogates and what is abrogated [nâsikh and mansûkh], what is fixed and what is ambiguous [mohkam and motashâbih], what applies particularly and what applies generally. And he prayed to God to enlarge my understanding and memory. Since he prayed for me in this way, I have not forgotten a single verse of the Book or a single item of knowledge he dictated to me. Then he placed his hand upon my breast and asked God to fill my heart with knowledge and understanding, discernment and light” (Sharh, p. 440). 'Abdollâh ibn 'Abbâs, one of the Prophet's Companions most learned in Qur'anic interpretation, confessed that beside the Imam he felt like a small jar at the edge of the Ocean. The Imam declared that the books he could write explaining the Fâtiha (the Qur'an's first sura) would make a load for seventy camels (ibid.). Many more quotations could be given. They all point to the essentially religious origins of what is called Shiism. ↩

Kolaynî, Osûl, Hojjat, Chapter I, third hadîth, pp. 315–318. Here is the end of the account: “‘Amrû [Abû Marwân] fell silent. A moment later he turned to me and said: ‘Are you Hishâm ibn al-Hakam?’ I said: ‘No!’ — ‘Then are you one of his companions?’ — ‘No!’ — ‘Where are you from, then?’ — ‘I am from Kufa,’ I replied. — ‘Then you are Hishâm!’ He drew me into his arms, seated me in his own place, and said nothing more until I stood to leave. When Imam Ja'far heard this story, he laughed and asked: ‘O Hishâm! Who taught you all this?’ — ‘It is something I learned from you yourself,’ said Hishâm, ‘and then put together afresh.’ The Imam replied: ‘God is my witness! The truth of what you have said is written in the Books of Abraham and Moses’ [Qur'an 87:19].” We hope to return elsewhere to the engaging figure of Hishâm ibn al-Hakam. As for the Mu'tazilite master 'Amrû ibn 'Obayd (d. 144/761), once a pupil of Hasan Basrî, see Mâmâqânî, Tanqîh al-Maqâl, vol. II, p. 334, no. 8729; and Rayhânat al-adab, under “Abû 'Othmân 'Amrû,” vol. V, p. 131, no. 225. It has become customary to emphasize certain points of agreement between Mu'tazilism and Shiism. Hishâm's encounter shows how far the two are from being in general agreement. Their spiritual tone differs. Even where they agree on points of kalâm (doctrinal theology), Shiite thought is not confined to kalâm: its fullest expression lies in hikmat ilâhîya (divine wisdom) and 'irfân (spiritual knowledge). ↩

Mulla Sadra, Sharh, p. 441. Compare the important discussion on pp. 261–262 (on Tawhid, chapter IX, seventh hadith, p. 178). Beyond sunlight, the brightest light in our world, there are other hidden, spiritual lights (anwar batiniya) that cannot be perceived by bodily sight: the more intense a light is, the less visible it becomes. These lights beyond the senses (malakutiya) form a hierarchy. At the lowest level is the life-giving, animating soul (nafs haywaniya), which the Qur'an (6:125) calls the sadr, the chest or breast (pectus). Above it is the thinking soul (nafs natiqa), called the heart (qalb) in religious language. Higher still is the contemplative intellect (aql nazari), which religious language calls the Spirit (ruh). Finally comes what the mystics (urafa) call the sirr, a level of awareness beyond ordinary consciousness, and what philosophers call the Active Intelligence (aql fa''al). All these correspondences deserve closer study. The last two lights may be compared to Fire and Air in our world of physical elements. Because they are so exalted, they have no outward form of manifestation (mazhar) in our world and no connection to a body of any kind, whether heavenly or earthly. The first two, being closer to our world, do have forms in which they become visible. The “animating souls” manifest in living earthly bodies and in the sadr (chest) of the human world in miniature. The greatest of these manifestations is also the greatest individual expression of the Soul of the World: it is the heaven of the firmament (Kursi). The thinking soul, by contrast, is the spiritual heart (qalb ma'nawi). Its earthly manifestations (mazahir) are human hearts—at least those of people “who have a heart” (50:36), that is, an Imam. “The greatest of all these forms is the Throne (arsh), the heart of the greater world. It is the place where the Light of Thought appears, and this Light is the seat of the name al-Rahman (the Merciful), the form in which God's hidden secret (sirr) becomes manifest...” ↩

Anything heard from outside [masmû'] is entirely useless when inborn intelligence is absent, just as sunlight is useless when the eye's power of sight is paralysed” (Sharh, p. 445). ↩

Mollâ Sadrâ quotes several Qur'anic verses in support. “We showed Abraham the Malakût of the heavens and the earth” (6:75); clearly this is not an outward perception. “The heart did not deny what it saw” (53:11, concerning the Prophet's first visionary experience): the heart's perception (idrâk al-qalb) is explicitly called vision (ru'ya). The opposite of knowledge is therefore blindness. Hence the verse: “It is not their eyes that are blind; it is their hearts, within their breasts, that are blind” (22:45). ↩

Osûl, Hojjat, Chapter III, first hadîth, pp. 329–330. Here Mollâ Sadrâ (Sharh, pp. 449–452) develops an extensive account of “prophetic philosophy.” He begins with scientific preliminaries of extraordinary interest, linking every recognized form of sacred, revealed knowledge (hierognosis) with the understanding of mind and bodily life commonly accepted in Islamic esotericism. His theory of knowledge is especially well suited to explaining such experiences because it begins from the principle that “every sensory perception, every perception possessing reality, does not at all mean that the soul sees a form existing in external matter. That external form is not the object of sensory perception, nor is it what becomes present to the perceiving soul. Rather, the essential object of sensory perception consists of the forms the soul sees with the eye of imaginative consciousness. External forms are causes that bring before imaginative consciousness a form corresponding to them symbolically [yomâthilo-hâ]. Thus what is truly perceived by the senses is the symbolic form shaped within representation, while what is external is called perceptible in another sense.” Mollâ Sadrâ can therefore readily explain that the symbolic or representative form (sûrat motamaththila) arises before imaginative consciousness in fundamentally the same way whether it is occasioned from outside and approached through the sense organs, or occasioned from within and brought into presence through the imaginative faculty's power to make spiritual realities knowable. In both cases there is vision. The point of this theory of knowledge is therefore not to place the “imaginary,” as something unreal, on one side and sensible objects, as the sole objects of true perception, on the other. It begins by recognizing the priority of the imaginative faculty, then distinguishes the processes leading to true vision from the disturbances or disorders producing hallucinations (or what we might call schizophrenia). All this is extraordinarily important. Mollâ Sadrâ takes the only critical position compatible with a prophetic theory of knowledge. We should also stress how Avicenna's theory of knowledge bore fruit through Suhrawardî's philosophy of Illumination (Ishrâq). ↩

Ibid., second hadîth, p. 330. Mollâ Sadrâ's pages on this hadîth and the next (Sharh, pp. 452 ff.) could form the basis of a substantial study of the archangel Gabriel's role in Islamic spirituality. Our authors know the derivation of his name (the names ending in -el). “Gabriel is the one called the Holy Spirit, the Initiator of mighty strength [an allusion to Qur'an 53:5], who gives aid by casting divine revelation into the prophets, inspiration into the Friends of God [Awliyâ], and truthful dream-visions into spiritual people. He is the Faithful Spirit, the Noble Messenger, whose virtues are countless and whose received gift is universal, as the verse says: ‘The Qur'an is the word of the Noble Messenger, who has power before the Master of the Throne and is firm, obeyed, faithful’ [81:19–21].” “When we speak of the Angel's speech [taklîm] and the account he gives [tahdîth], we mean something that happens in the innermost depth of consciousness [fî bâtin al-sirr], as spiritual speech [kalâm 'aqlî] and spiritual communication [hadîth rûhânî]. That is why Gabriel is called the Holy Spirit [Rûh al-Qods]: in himself he is a sacred essence, so long as he has not descended from the heaven of his transcendence and nearness to God. When he descends from that rank of divine nearness, he takes on a figure and assumes a particular form corresponding to the person upon whom he descends” (Sharh, p. 453). ↩

Sharh, p. 452. On this central theme in Mollâ Sadrâ's work, see Book V, Chapter II below. Prophetic knowledge forms a coherent whole: the reality of the mundus imaginalis ('âlam al-mithâl), the capacity of imaginative perception to convey knowledge, and its spiritual nature, independent of the physical body and constituting something like the soul's subtle body. ↩

Osûl, Hojjat, Chapter III, fourth hadîth, p. 331. This tradition, from the Fifth and Sixth Imams, is noteworthy, among other reasons, because it tells us that the Qur'anic text used by the Imams included, at 22:51, the words: “Before you We sent neither a messenger nor a prophet nor a mohaddath [one spoken to by the angels] …” The standard Qur'anic text today does not contain the third term (see already the first hadîth in this chapter). The received Qur'anic text, that is, the edition of 'Othmân, is held to have been purged of passages favourable to Shiism. This seems to offer a particularly clear indication. Note also that the concept and title of the “Seal” (khâtim) of prophecy explicitly occur in the Imams' teachings. ↩

Ibid., third hadîth, pp. 330–331, from the Fifth Imam: “The rasûl [Messenger] is the one to whom Gabriel appears face to face; he sees him and speaks with him. The nabî [prophet] is the one who has dream-visions like Abraham's, and like those experienced by God's Messenger before revelation [wahy], until Gabriel came to him from God bearing the risâlat [the commission of a prophet who proclaims a Law] […]. As for the mohaddath, he is the one to whom the Angel speaks; he hears the Angel without seeing him in a dream.” This is exactly the case of the Imam as defined by the Fifth Imam in the first hadîth of the same chapter and by the Eighth Imam in the second (above, pp. 241 ff., nn. 222 and 223): “The Imam hears the Angel's words without seeing the Angel himself.” It is important to observe that mohaddath (“one addressed by angels”) is defined within the Shiite teaching about the Imams, and by the Imams themselves. ↩

That is why, before the Prophet of Islam, an ordinary nabî could rank above a Messenger: “Do you not see that Khezr [Khadir] was a nabî, not a rasûl? Yet it was he who initiated Moses, although Moses was one of the greatest Messengers, being a prophet who brought a Law. Or, to put it more precisely: the dimension [jihat] of prophecy [nobowwat] in a rasûl is higher than the dimension of his risâlat [the prophetic mission directed toward others], because the former is the perfection of the contemplative intellect, while the latter is the perfection of the practical intellect” (Sharh, p. 449). Khezr is the mysterious prophet paired with Elijah or identified with him. Certain Shiite groups have identified him with the Twelfth Imam.
